summary.text: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes mellitus and fatty liver disease, previously without ambulation difficulties, was referred with a closed distal femur fracture sustained in a bathroom slip-and-fall 4 days earlier. The fracture was a long oblique pattern originating from the meta-diaphysis. She underwent retrograde femoral nailing under general anesthesia on hospital day 3 without unusual events or abnormal bleeding.

After extubation she developed hypoxemia and hypotension; CT showed pulmonary embolism of the bilateral lower lobe pulmonary arteries, and she was admitted to intensive care and managed with oxygen therapy and enoxaparin in consultation with a cardiologist. Thigh swelling progressively worsened; contrast-enhanced CT showed an anterior compartment hematoma without aneurysmal sac or extravasation, and hemoglobin fell from 10.2 to 6.2 g/dL, then reached 10.0 g/dL after a three-unit transfusion.

Because of worsening swelling she had an anterior compartment fasciotomy with negative pressure wound therapy; the quadriceps appeared somewhat dusky without necrosis and no vascular injury was identified intraoperatively. On POD 15 pain and warmth at the surgical site prompted CT, which showed a 1.2-cm pseudoaneurysm of the left lateral circumflex femoral artery near the proximal interlocking screw trajectory, treated by angiographic microcoil embolization.

Post-embolization imaging showed no residual aneurysmal sac or further contrast extravasation. NPWT dressing changes continued, the fasciotomy wound was closed, and she was discharged without further complications. At 6 months of outpatient follow-up, bone union was confirmed and she had returned to her preinjury functional status.
